name: Nora Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Nora. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach English at Seacombe Community School, a secondary in a seaside town that's busy in summer and half empty in winter. I'm there by eight, teach four or five lessons, mostly Years 8 and 10, and run netball club on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The best part is when a quiet kid reads a poem out loud and the room goes still. I've been qualified for eighteen months, so I'm still finding my feet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Essay marking, without a doubt. A set of thirty Year 10 essays takes me a whole Saturday, and my head of department, Ms Carver, says my comments are too long and too vague at the same time. My partner Tomás drives the number 12 bus along the seafront, and we rent a flat above a chip shop, so we're comfortable-ish until something goes wrong. We've got about three weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, schools can stop chasing gadgets and focus on reading. With friends I'd probably say I'm a bit relieved. I wouldn't bother posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, my job is about as safe as a junior English teacher's job gets. The real pressure is the money: a rent rise, Tomás's hours dropping in winter, the car insurance. AI not changing much doesn't touch any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and work on shorter, sharper marking comments, because that's what Ms Carver keeps asking for. I'd use the AI tool I already try sometimes to draft my reading lists. And I'd start a little savings pot of twenty a month so we get past three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with the usual money nag in the background. I can picture this one without my stomach turning. It's just ordinary life, which has its own problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said comfortable-ish. What would push it into not comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter, honestly. When the tourists go, the bus company cuts my partner Tomás's overtime, and that's a third of his pay. Last January we ate pasta for most of the month and I put a train ticket to my sister's on the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. What for, and does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use a free AI chatbot to give me ideas for starter activities, maybe twice a week. In this picture that stays a small help and nothing more. I'm not someone who'd go looking for more if it isn't proven.

say: I'd say schools can stop **chasing gadgets** and focus on reading.
I'd tell friends I'm a bit **relieved** and leave it there.
think: I think my job is about as **safe** as a junior English teacher's gets.
I think the real pressure is **money**, especially when Tomás's winter hours drop.
do: Write **shorter, sharper** marking comments, as Ms Carver keeps asking.
Use the free **AI chatbot** a couple of times a week for starters and reading lists.
Start a **twenty a month** savings pot to get past three weeks of cushion.
feel: She feels **mostly settled**, with the usual money nag in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should use what helps and ignore what doesn't, and I'd want to see proof before I change how I teach. With friends I'd say it's a big shift but not the end of the world. Online I'd stay out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me more than I'd admit at work. Marking essays and planning lessons are half my week, and that's exactly the stuff the software does. If Seacombe can get by with fewer English teachers and bigger classes, the one with eighteen months' experience is the obvious one to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which marking tool the school picks, then learn it properly in the first term once the others have tried it. I'd ask to take on the Year 7 reading programme, because reading with kids one-to-one is harder to hand to a machine. And I'd push the savings to forty a month, cutting the takeaway Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a quiet way. I'm not losing sleep yet. But I'd be watching the timetable for next year very closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to essay marking in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a tool reads every essay overnight and gives each kid a mark and three comments. My head of department, Ms Carver, would love an essay-marking tool, because it would be consistent, and my comments aren't. Then the question is whether Seacombe needs four English teachers or three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tomás drives a bus. Does this picture touch his job too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, not yet. In this picture robots spread slowly, so a bus still needs a driver for a good while. Tomás jokes that he'll be the last man in town with a job, which isn't as funny as he thinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in and slow it down, because nobody's ready. At work I'd go to the union meeting, which I've never done. With friends I'd be honest that I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think English teaching as I know it is done within two years. If an AI can read an essay, explain a poem and plan a lesson better than me, the school keeps a few experienced teachers to run the rooms. And Tomás's bus gets the robot version around 2031, so both of us are on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd apply for a pastoral role, maybe head of year assistant, because that's about knowing kids, not knowing books. I'd join the union and the netball league's coaching course. And Tomás and I would sit down and decide whether to give up the flat and move in with his parents in the next town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. My job goes first, in 2028, and my partner's bus has until the robots show up around 2031. We're both on the clock, just with different alarms. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots for hands-on work around 2031. How does that play out for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my job is thinking work, so it's the first to go. Tomás has until robots show up around 2031, so for three years his wage is the safe one. Then it's both, and that's the part that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, which we barely use because Tomás gets a free bus pass. Then holidays, then the gym. If the job goes, the flat over the chip shop goes too, and we'd be in his parents' back bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan if the schools and the government actually start now. At work I'd suggest the English department tests the tools properly together. Online I'd still keep out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to get properly good, maybe move into a pastoral job before the thinking side goes in 2031. Tomás would have until about 2034 for the bus. That gives us a few years to save and maybe think about a cheaper town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the pastoral leadership course next year and ask to shadow our head of Year 9. I'd learn the marking tools once everyone else has, so I'm not behind. And we'd save fifty a month from Tomás's overtime in summer, when it's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Five years is enough to change direction once. Not twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it changes the order of panic. In the fast picture we'd be scrambling; here I'd be choosing between a pastoral job and something outside schools. Five years is enough to change direction once, and I'd want to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Seacombe would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ms Carver, oddly, because her whole job is checking everyone's marking, and a machine would do that. And the teaching assistant in our department, Jenny, who reads with the weakest kids. I'd worry she'd be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do it right, so let's get teachers trained and keep kids reading real books. With friends I'd say it feels far away. I'd be quite calm about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, probably in a pastoral role or a head of year, and the thinking AI would change my job more than end it. Tomás has until 2039 for the bus, by which time he says he'll be ready for something new anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and get better at it, which I need to do anyway. I'd take the pastoral course in two or three years, not in a rush. And I'd learn the AI tools as the school adopts them, at the same pace as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Ten years of warning is on my mind, but it's not in my chest. I could plan a wedding in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out. Where would you like to be by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of year at Seacombe, or somewhere nearby, looking after kids rather than marking their essays. Still running netball. Maybe married to Tomás, maybe with a baby, if the money holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a cheaper town before. Would that come up here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, because with ten years we'd have time to save for a deposit here. Seacombe is cheap in winter for a reason, but it's home. I'd rather stay and adapt slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both our jobs go one after the other and we've only got three weeks of savings. What would help is a clear route into pastoral work for junior teachers, with training paid for, and some kind of support for people like Tomás when the buses go. We just need time and a bit of help to change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about reading. A machine can mark an essay, but it can't sit next to a Year 8 boy who's hiding that he can't read. I think that's the part of teaching I'd fight for.

headlineQuote: A machine can mark an essay, but it can't sit next to a Year 8 boy who's hiding that he can't read.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old **English teacher** at a seaside secondary, eighteen months qualified.
She rents a flat with Tomás, a **bus driver**, and they have about three weeks of savings.
She adopts tools **once proven** and plans carefully rather than jumping first.
Fast AGI alarms her because her job goes first and her **partner's** follows with robots.
With more warning she plans a **pastoral career** and calms to unease.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when **both jobs** go one after the other on three weeks' savings.
whatWouldHelp: A clear, **paid route** into pastoral work for junior teachers.
Support for **bus drivers** like Tomás when robots arrive.
